Reference: Longuet-Marx (2026)

Model Setting

The paper asks why less-educated (blue-collar) voters in the United States have moved away from the Democratic Party while college graduates have moved toward it: over twenty years the share of voters with a high school diploma or less who support the Democrats fell by more than 10 percentage points and the share of college graduates who do so rose by a similar amount. The literature is split between demand-side explanations (voters' preferences and demographics changed) and supply-side explanations (parties changed what they offer). The paper estimates a political equilibrium model of U.S. House elections from 2000 to 2020 in which heterogeneous voters choose between a Democratic candidate, a Republican candidate and abstention, and the two candidates of each district choose positions on a cultural and an economic dimension, trading off the probability of winning against the cost of deviating from the national party leadership. Four objects can change between 2000-2010 and 2012-2020: voter preferences, voter demographics, the positions of party leaders, and party discipline. The model is solved under all combinations of initial and final values of these objects to attribute the change in the education gap in Democratic voting to each of them.

Three ingredients are new. Candidate positions for winners and losers are estimated from candidate surveys and campaign websites with a multimodal text-and-survey ideal point model. Voter demand is estimated on a new panel of precinct-level election results (1.6 million observations, about 175,000 precincts per year, about 400 precincts per congressional district), which makes it possible to compare adjacent precincts on the two sides of a congressional district border. Candidate supply is estimated from the first-order condition of the positioning game given the estimated demand. The main findings are these. Less-educated voters prefer conservative cultural positions and progressive economic positions, and their taste for progressive economic positions has grown. The parties polarized much more on cultural than on economic issues, with two thirds of the widening gap driven by the Democratic Party. Party discipline rose sharply in both parties. In equilibrium, the cultural polarization of party leaders is the main force that widened the education gap, while the change in voter preferences worked in the opposite direction: without it, realignment would have been even more pronounced.

Conceptual Framework

The model is a static game of local political competition. In district ddd and election year ttt there is a set of voters Idt\mathcal{I}_{dt}Idt​, each voter iii having observable characteristics widt\mathbf{w}_{idt}widt​ (education, race, age). Two candidates j∈{D,R}j\in\{D,R\}j∈{D,R} choose platforms xjdt∈Rk\mathbf{x}_{jdt}\in\mathbb{R}^kxjdt​∈Rk. A voter who chooses candidate jjj obtains uijdt=vit(xjdt;widt)+εijdtu_{ijdt}=v_{it}(\mathbf{x}_{jdt};\mathbf{w}_{idt})+\varepsilon_{ijdt}uijdt​=vit​(xjdt​;widt​)+εijdt​ and a voter who abstains obtains ui0dt=εi0dtu_{i0dt}=\varepsilon_{i0dt}ui0dt​=εi0dt​, where the εijdt\varepsilon_{ijdt}εijdt​ are idiosyncratic i.i.d. mean-zero taste shocks. The individual choice probability is:

sijdt(xDdt,xRdt;widt)=Pr⁡(uijdt≥max⁡l∈{D,R,0}uildt)(1)s_{ijdt}\left(\mathbf{x}_{Ddt},\mathbf{x}_{Rdt};\mathbf{w}_{idt}\right)=\Pr\left(u_{ijdt}\geq\max_{l\in\{D,R,0\}}u_{ildt}\right) \tag{1}sijdt​(xDdt​,xRdt​;widt​)=Pr(uijdt​≥l∈{D,R,0}max​uildt​)(1)

and the vote share of alternative jjj integrates over the distribution Fdt(⋅)F_{dt}(\cdot)Fdt​(⋅) of voter characteristics in the district:

sjdt=∫sijdt(xDdt,xRdt;w)dFdt(w)(2)s_{jdt}=\int s_{ijdt}\left(\mathbf{x}_{Ddt},\mathbf{x}_{Rdt};\mathbf{w}\right)dF_{dt}(\mathbf{w}) \tag{2}sjdt​=∫sijdt​(xDdt​,xRdt​;w)dFdt​(w)(2)

Lowercase shares are model-implied, uppercase shares are observed, and a tilde denotes a share conditional on turnout. Each candidate derives a rent Q>0Q>0Q>0 from office and maximizes:

Πjdt(xjdt)=Pjdt(xjdt,x−jdt)Q−cjt(xjdt,Njt)(3)\Pi_{jdt}(\mathbf{x}_{jdt})=P_{jdt}(\mathbf{x}_{jdt},\mathbf{x}_{-jdt})Q-c_{jt}(\mathbf{x}_{jdt},\mathbf{N}_{jt}) \tag{3}Πjdt​(xjdt​)=Pjdt​(xjdt​,x−jdt​)Q−cjt​(xjdt​,Njt​)(3)

where PjdtP_{jdt}Pjdt​ is the probability of winning, which depends on the vote share conditional on turnout s~jdt\tilde{s}_{jdt}s~jdt​ and on a random shock, and cjt(⋅)c_{jt}(\cdot)cjt​(⋅) is the cost of deviating from the position Njt∈Rk\mathbf{N}_{jt}\in\mathbb{R}^kNjt​∈Rk of the national party leadership. The lower this cost, the more a candidate can adapt to local conditions. The need to comply with the leadership is not modelled explicitly; it stands for rewards that leaders give to loyal candidates before and after the election and for the cost of designing a local strategy. Leadership positions are treated as exogenous to any single district.

A Nash equilibrium in district-election (d,t)(d,t)(d,t) is a pair of positions (xDdt,xRdt)(\mathbf{x}_{Ddt},\mathbf{x}_{Rdt})(xDdt​,xRdt​) and vote shares (sDdt,sRdt,s0dt)(s_{Ddt},s_{Rdt},s_{0dt})(sDdt​,sRdt​,s0dt​) such that each xjdt\mathbf{x}_{jdt}xjdt​ maximizes Πjdt\Pi_{jdt}Πjdt​ given the opponent's position, and the shares satisfy the integral above for j∈{D,R,0}j\in\{D,R,0\}j∈{D,R,0}. The empirical goal is to decompose the change in voting between two periods into changes in sijdt(⋅)s_{ijdt}(\cdot)sijdt​(⋅) and Fdt(w)F_{dt}(\mathbf{w})Fdt​(w) on the demand side and changes in Nt=(NDt,NRt)\mathbf{N}_t=(\mathbf{N}_{Dt},\mathbf{N}_{Rt})Nt​=(NDt​,NRt​) and cjt(⋅)c_{jt}(\cdot)cjt​(⋅) on the supply side. Leadership positions affect votes only through the positions that local candidates choose: utility does not depend on Njt\mathbf{N}_{jt}Njt​ directly.

Data and Realignment Facts

Precinct-level House results for 2000-2020 are assembled from more than 100 sources (six existing archives, plus Secretaries of State and county officials). Because precinct boundaries change, votes are apportioned to 2010 census block-groups through the spatial overlap of precincts and census blocks, and the block-group is called a precinct throughout. Only states available both before and after 2010 are kept. Turnout is total votes over the population aged 18 or older. Census and American Community Survey data give block-group demographics; since only marginal distributions are published, the joint distribution of education, race and age in each block-group is recovered from a multi-scale model that combines block-group and tract counts with individual data at the PUMA level. In the resulting individual-level distribution, mean schooling is 13.45 years with a standard deviation of 3.56 (2.87 within precincts), mean age is 48.91, and 74 percent of individuals are white (non-Hispanic, single race). Union membership (from contract-level data of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service) and church membership are also built at the block-group level.

Realignment is compared across M=12M=12M=12 standardized demographic variables in one regression:

S~Dpt=∑m=1Mβmwm,pt⋅t+∑m=1Mγmwm,pt+μt+εpt(4)\tilde{S}_{Dpt}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\beta_mw_{m,pt}\cdot t+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\gamma_mw_{m,pt}+\mu_t+\varepsilon_{pt} \tag{4}S~Dpt​=m=1∑M​βm​wm,pt​⋅t+m=1∑M​γm​wm,pt​+μt​+εpt​(4)

where S~Dpt\tilde{S}_{Dpt}S~Dpt​ is the Democratic House vote share in precinct ppp at election ttt conditional on turnout, wm,ptw_{m,pt}wm,pt​ is demographic dimension mmm, and μt\mu_tμt​ are election fixed effects. A positive βm\beta_mβm​ is a realignment toward the Democrats. Education has the largest coefficient in absolute value, three times that of income; the share of white residents and the share of rural residents follow, with shifts toward the Republicans. The result holds with demographics fixed at 2000 values and with precinct fixed effects. In each successive election the education gap between Democratic and Republican voters grows by 2.5 months of schooling, and the trend predates 2016. Across precincts the relationship between education and the Democratic share is U-shaped: in 2020 the covariance of 0.005 is the sum of a within-district covariance of −0.012-0.012−0.012 and a between-district covariance of 0.017.

Measuring Candidate Positions

Positions come from Project VoteSmart candidate surveys and from campaign websites archived by the Library of Congress the day before the general election (available from 2002). There are 132 distinct questions asked in at least two cycles, in 15 topics. Employment, trade, taxes, health care, social security and welfare form the economic dimension; abortion, crime, education, environment, guns, campaign finance, immigration, security and international policy, and diversity form the cultural dimension. The signs of the demand estimates imply that higher values of a position are more conservative. Suppressing the district index, let yjqty_{jqt}yjqt​ be the response of candidate jjj to item qqq in period ttt and xjktx_{jkt}xjkt​ the latent position on dimension kkk. Binary items follow a two-parameter logistic item-response model:

Pr⁡(yjqt=1∣xjkt,αq,βq)=11+exp⁡[−αq(xjkt−βq)](5)\Pr\left(y_{jqt}=1\mid x_{jkt},\alpha_q,\beta_q\right)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\left[-\alpha_q\left(x_{jkt}-\beta_q\right)\right]} \tag{5}Pr(yjqt​=1∣xjkt​,αq​,βq​)=1+exp[−αq​(xjkt​−βq​)]1​(5)

where βq\beta_qβq​ is the cut-point at which a yes has probability one half and αq>0\alpha_q>0αq​>0 is the discrimination parameter. Ordered items with CqC_qCq​ categories follow a graded response model:

Pr⁡(yjqt≥c∣xjkt,αq,δq)=11+exp⁡[−αq(xjkt−δqc)],c=1,…,Cq−1(6)\Pr\left(y_{jqt}\geq c\mid x_{jkt},\alpha_q,\delta_q\right)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\left[-\alpha_q\left(x_{jkt}-\delta_{qc}\right)\right]},\qquad c=1,\ldots,C_q-1 \tag{6}Pr(yjqt​≥c∣xjkt​,αq​,δq​)=1+exp[−αq​(xjkt​−δqc​)]1​,c=1,…,Cq​−1(6)

with ordered cut-points δq1<⋯<δq,Cq−1\delta_{q1}<\cdots<\delta_{q,C_q-1}δq1​<⋯<δq,Cq​−1​; category probabilities are differences of adjacent cumulative probabilities. Positions are dynamic:

xjkt=ρkxjk,t−1+σkηjkt,ηjkt∼N(0,1)ρk=2−1/hk,σk=1−ρk2(7)\begin{aligned} x_{jkt}&=\rho_kx_{jk,t-1}+\sigma_k\eta_{jkt},\qquad\eta_{jkt}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\\ \rho_k&=2^{-1/h_k},\qquad\sigma_k=\sqrt{1-\rho_k^2} \end{aligned} \tag{7}xjkt​ρk​​=ρk​xjk,t−1​+σk​ηjkt​,ηjkt​∼N(0,1)=2−1/hk​,σk​=1−ρk2​​​(7)

where hkh_khk​ is the half-life of a shock, estimated with a log-normal prior centred on one election cycle, and the restriction on σk\sigma_kσk​ makes the process stationary with unit variance, so positions are measured in standard deviations. The model is estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo; the posterior mean is the survey ideal point and the posterior standard deviation its standard error. A gradient-boosting regressor is then trained to predict survey ideal points from website text (n-grams and document embeddings), with a mean squared error of 0.17 on the economic and 0.21 on the cultural dimension. The two measures are combined by their relative precision:

xjdkt=ωjdktxjdktsurvey+(1−ωjdkt)xjdktwebsiteωjdkt=MSEkwebsitese(xjdktsurvey)2+MSEkwebsite(8)\begin{aligned} x_{jdkt}&=\omega_{jdkt}x^{survey}_{jdkt}+\left(1-\omega_{jdkt}\right)x^{website}_{jdkt}\\ \omega_{jdkt}&=\frac{MSE^{website}_k}{se\left(x^{survey}_{jdkt}\right)^2+MSE^{website}_k} \end{aligned} \tag{8}xjdkt​ωjdkt​​=ωjdkt​xjdktsurvey​+(1−ωjdkt​)xjdktwebsite​=se(xjdktsurvey​)2+MSEkwebsite​MSEkwebsite​​​(8)

About 49 percent of candidates have both measures, 32 percent only the survey and 7 percent only the website; the remaining 12 percent are dropped. Survey and website measures correlate above 0.9 overall and above 0.7 within party. The leadership position Njt\mathbf{N}_{jt}Njt​ is the average position of the Speaker, the Majority and Minority Leaders, the Whips and the Chairs of the Caucus and the Conference.

The rank correlation between the two dimensions is 0.89 overall but only 0.57 among Democrats and 0.41 among Republicans, and the within-party correlations fell from 0.62 and 0.48 in 2000-2010 to 0.43 and 0.28 in 2012-2020. The average distance between Democratic and Republican candidates rose from 1.63 to 2.07 on cultural issues and stayed flat on economic issues (1.89 and 1.87). Across districts, candidates of both parties are more culturally progressive where voters are more educated, and, conditional on the cultural position, more economically conservative, which suggests that candidates respond to constituents.

Voter Demand

Voter iii in precinct ppp of district ddd who chooses candidate j∈{D,R}j\in\{D,R\}j∈{D,R} in election ttt obtains:

uijpt=∑kβiktxjdkt+αijt+ξjpt+εijpt(9)u_{ijpt}=\sum_k\beta_{ikt}x_{jdkt}+\alpha_{ijt}+\xi_{jpt}+\varepsilon_{ijpt} \tag{9}uijpt​=k∑​βikt​xjdkt​+αijt​+ξjpt​+εijpt​(9)

where xjdktx_{jdkt}xjdkt​ is the position of candidate jjj on dimension kkk, αijt\alpha_{ijt}αijt​ is the utility of voting for party jjj independently of positions, ξjpt\xi_{jpt}ξjpt​ is a party-specific precinct-level taste shock, and εijpt\varepsilon_{ijpt}εijpt​ is type-I extreme value. Abstention gives ui0pt=εi0ptu_{i0pt}=\varepsilon_{i0pt}ui0pt​=εi0pt​. Preferences are heterogeneous:

αijt=αjt+wit′αjtwβikt=βkt+wit′βktw+σktβνkit(10)\begin{aligned} \alpha_{ijt}&=\alpha_{jt}+\mathbf{w}'_{it}\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{w}}_{jt}\\ \beta_{ikt}&=\beta_{kt}+\mathbf{w}'_{it}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}+\sigma^{\beta}_{kt}\nu_{kit} \end{aligned} \tag{10}αijt​βikt​​=αjt​+wit′​αjtw​=βkt​+wit′​βktw​+σktβ​νkit​​(10)

where wit\mathbf{w}_{it}wit​ contains years of schooling, race and age, αjtw\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{w}}_{jt}αjtw​ and βktw\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}βktw​ describe how partisan and ideological preferences vary with demographics, and νkit\nu_{kit}νkit​ is residual heterogeneity with νit∼Pν=N(0,IK)\boldsymbol{\nu}_{it}\sim P_\nu=\mathcal{N}(0,I_K)νit​∼Pν​=N(0,IK​) and scale σktβ\sigma^{\beta}_{kt}σktβ​. The utility is linear in positions, so βikt\beta_{ikt}βikt​ is the marginal utility of a more conservative position on dimension kkk and not a distance to an ideal point. The precinct vote share of candidate jjj integrates the random-coefficients logit probability over unobserved heterogeneity and over the distribution Fpt(⋅)F_{pt}(\cdot)Fpt​(⋅) of demographics in the precinct:

sjpt=∫∫exp⁡(∑kβiktxjdkt+αijt+ξjpt)1+∑l∈{D,R}exp⁡(∑kβiktxldkt+αilt+ξlpt)dPνdFpt(w)(11)s_{jpt}=\int\int\frac{\exp\left(\sum_k\beta_{ikt}x_{jdkt}+\alpha_{ijt}+\xi_{jpt}\right)}{1+\sum_{l\in\{D,R\}}\exp\left(\sum_k\beta_{ikt}x_{ldkt}+\alpha_{ilt}+\xi_{lpt}\right)}dP_\nu dF_{pt}(\mathbf{w}) \tag{11}sjpt​=∫∫1+∑l∈{D,R}​exp(∑k​βikt​xldkt​+αilt​+ξlpt​)exp(∑k​βikt​xjdkt​+αijt​+ξjpt​)​dPν​dFpt​(w)(11)

Following Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995), the shocks ξjpt\xi_{jpt}ξjpt​ are obtained by inverting the share equations so that model shares equal observed shares, and the parameters are estimated by GMM with the PyBLP package of Conlon and Gortmaker (2023). The term αijt\alpha_{ijt}αijt​ absorbs non-ideological party attachment and the coattails of presidential and Senate candidates; it is treated as a control and receives no structural interpretation. Separate models are estimated for 2000-2010 and 2012-2020. If voters are assumed homogeneous within precincts, wit=wpt\mathbf{w}_{it}=\mathbf{w}_{pt}wit​=wpt​, and there are no random coefficients, the model reduces to the logit of Berry (1994):

log⁡(SjptS0pt)=αjt+wpt′αjtw+∑k(βktxjdkt+wpt′βktwxjdkt)+ξjpt(12)\log\left(\frac{S_{jpt}}{S_{0pt}}\right)=\alpha_{jt}+\mathbf{w}'_{pt}\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{w}}_{jt}+\sum_k\left(\beta_{kt}x_{jdkt}+\mathbf{w}'_{pt}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}x_{jdkt}\right)+\xi_{jpt} \tag{12}log(S0pt​Sjpt​​)=αjt​+wpt′​αjtw​+k∑​(βkt​xjdkt​+wpt′​βktw​xjdkt​)+ξjpt​(12)

which is estimated by OLS with the same fixed effects as a robustness check.

Identification of Demand

Candidate positions are chosen with knowledge of district-level tastes, so they are correlated with ξjpt\xi_{jpt}ξjpt​. The solution uses the hierarchy of the data: positions are set at the district level and votes are observed at the precinct level, and a single precinct is about one four-hundredth of a district. The taste shock is decomposed as:

ξjpt=ξjg(p)t+ξjp+ξ~jpt(13)\xi_{jpt}=\xi_{jg(p)t}+\xi_{jp}+\tilde{\xi}_{jpt} \tag{13}ξjpt​=ξjg(p)t​+ξjp​+ξ~​jpt​(13)

where ξjg(p)t\xi_{jg(p)t}ξjg(p)t​ is a party-specific shock common at election ttt to the precincts of the same border group g(p)g(p)g(p) on both sides of a district border, ξjp\xi_{jp}ξjp​ is a time-invariant precinct-party component, and ξ~jpt\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}ξ~​jpt​ is the residual. The first two components are absorbed by precinct-group-by-party-by-election and precinct-by-party fixed effects. The identifying assumption is that candidate positions are uncorrelated with the residual, and the first-step moments, for each dimension kkk, each demographic characteristic wptw_{pt}wpt​ (schooling, race, age and interactions) and each party jjj, are:

E[xjdkt⋅ξ~jpt]=0E[(xjdkt⋅wpt)⋅ξ~jpt]=0E[wpt⋅ξ~jpt]=0E[xjdkt2⋅ξ~jpt]=0E[(xjdkt2⋅wpt)⋅ξ~jpt]=0E[(xDdkt−xRdkt)⋅ξ~jpt]=0E[((xDdkt−xRdkt)⋅wpt)⋅ξ~jpt]=0(14)\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left[x_{jdkt}\cdot\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}\right]&=0\\ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(x_{jdkt}\cdot w_{pt}\right)\cdot\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}\right]&=0\\ \mathbb{E}\left[w_{pt}\cdot\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}\right]&=0\\ \mathbb{E}\left[x^2_{jdkt}\cdot\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}\right]&=0\\ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(x^2_{jdkt}\cdot w_{pt}\right)\cdot\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}\right]&=0\\ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(x_{Ddkt}-x_{Rdkt}\right)\cdot\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}\right]&=0\\ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(x_{Ddkt}-x_{Rdkt}\right)\cdot w_{pt}\right)\cdot\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}\right]&=0 \end{aligned} \tag{14}E[xjdkt​⋅ξ~​jpt​]E[(xjdkt​⋅wpt​)⋅ξ~​jpt​]E[wpt​⋅ξ~​jpt​]E[xjdkt2​⋅ξ~​jpt​]E[(xjdkt2​⋅wpt​)⋅ξ~​jpt​]E[(xDdkt​−xRdkt​)⋅ξ~​jpt​]E[((xDdkt​−xRdkt​)⋅wpt​)⋅ξ~​jpt​]​=0=0=0=0=0=0=0​(14)

Positions therefore instrument for themselves once the fixed effects are removed: the variation is the change over time in the difference between the candidates faced by adjacent precincts on opposite sides of a border. The squared positions, the distance between the two candidates and the interactions with demographics identify the random-coefficient scales and the demographic gradients. The model uses no micro moments from surveys; individual heterogeneity is identified from the within-precinct distribution of demographics and from the variation in choice sets, and survey data are used only for validation. Only borders within a state are used, so legislation and upper-level races are the same on both sides. Border precincts are assembled into geographically contiguous cross-border groups of at most 5 precincts (median 3) by an assignment algorithm that minimizes rank-based proximity costs; 16 percent of precincts touch a district border. In a balance test, precinct demographics are strongly correlated with candidate positions in OLS but not after the fixed effects: one of 20 coefficients is significant at the 10 percent level, and the joint F-statistics are 1.06 (p=0.39p=0.39p=0.39) for cultural and 0.50 (p=0.89p=0.89p=0.89) for economic positions.

The first step removes the variation that identifies party preferences, since demographics are nearly identical within a group (wpt≈wg(p)tw_{pt}\approx w_{g(p)t}wpt​≈wg(p)t​). Party affiliation is taken as exogenous, so the second step uses the full sample, holds the first-step ideological parameters fixed, and recovers the demographic heterogeneity of αijt\alpha_{ijt}αijt​ from:

E[wpt⋅ξjpt]=0(15)\mathbb{E}\left[w_{pt}\cdot\xi_{jpt}\right]=0 \tag{15}E[wpt​⋅ξjpt​]=0(15)

Second-step standard errors are corrected for first-step uncertainty following Murphy and Topel (1985). In 216 Monte Carlo simulations, the precinct-level random-coefficients model recovers all parameters with small bias (for example −0.018-0.018−0.018 on a true βcult\beta_{cult}βcult​ of 0.25), while the homogeneous logit and both county-level versions are badly biased (the county-level random-coefficients model has a bias of −4.2-4.2−4.2 on a true βecon\beta_{econ}βecon​ of −0.4-0.4−0.4).

Demand Estimates

Standard errors, in parentheses, are clustered by congressional district by election.

  • Education gradient: the coefficient βedu,cult\beta_{edu,cult}βedu,cult​ on the interaction of the cultural position with years of schooling is −0.0190-0.0190−0.0190 (0.0045) in 2000-2010 and −0.0185-0.0185−0.0185 (0.0037) in 2012-2020, so more-educated voters prefer more progressive cultural positions and the gradient is stable. The economic counterpart βedu,econ\beta_{edu,econ}βedu,econ​ rises from 0.0060 (0.0040) to 0.0159 (0.0035): less-educated voters prefer more progressive economic positions than more-educated voters, and this gradient becomes comparable in size to the cultural one.

  • Baseline coefficients: βcult\beta_{cult}βcult​ is 0.2762 (0.0722) and then 0.1663 (0.0613); βecon\beta_{econ}βecon​ is −0.0324-0.0324−0.0324 (0.0674) and then −0.2391-0.2391−0.2391 (0.0633), a shift of all voters toward progressive economic positions.

  • Race and age: the interactions with the white indicator are −0.0611-0.0611−0.0611 (0.0311) and −0.0430-0.0430−0.0430 (0.0211) on the cultural dimension and −0.0181-0.0181−0.0181 (0.0270) and −0.0565-0.0565−0.0565 (0.0245) on the economic dimension. Older voters prefer more conservative cultural positions in the second period, 0.0034 (0.0010), and age does not matter on the economic dimension.

  • Unobserved heterogeneity: σcultβ\sigma^{\beta}_{cult}σcultβ​ is 0.0477 (0.0136) and then 0.0581 (0.0126); σeconβ\sigma^{\beta}_{econ}σeconβ​ is 0.0017 (0.0076) and then 0.0147 (0.0086).

  • Party preferences: the interaction of the Democratic indicator with schooling rises from 0.0895 (0.0186) to 0.2990 (0.0184) and that with the white indicator falls from −3.7737-3.7737−3.7737 (0.1576) to −4.4093-4.4093−4.4093 (0.1486); the Democratic intercept moves from 1.1942 to −0.8827-0.8827−0.8827. More-educated, white and older voters are more likely to turn out in both periods.

  • Validation: model-based probabilities of voting Democratic for 12 groups defined by race, education and age correlate with ANES and CCES self-reports at 0.87 (2000-2010) and 0.94 (2012-2020) in levels and 0.96 in changes. The homogeneous logit gives similar gradients (cultural position times schooling −0.028-0.028−0.028 and −0.023-0.023−0.023; economic position times schooling 0.003 and 0.056, in standardized units), and adding incumbency, gender and race of the candidate leaves the results quantitatively similar.

The estimates are summarized by an education-neutral curve in the plane of economic and cultural polarization (the distance between the Democratic and the Republican position on each dimension): the combinations at which less-educated voters (below the national median, 13.65 years of schooling in 2020) and more-educated voters vote Democratic at the same rate. When the parties are far apart on economic issues and close on cultural issues, Democrats do relatively better among the less educated; when cultural polarization is large relative to economic polarization, they do relatively better among the more educated. Between 2000 and 2020 the leadership positions moved from the curve into the second region. The curve based on 2012-2020 preferences is steeper: Democrats need less economic polarization per unit of cultural polarization to retain less-educated voters, so the preference change offset part of the loss. The paper reports no vote-share elasticities with respect to positions.

Candidate Supply

The supply side is a candidate competition model in the tradition of Wittman (1983). The cost of deviation is quadratic and the objective is:

Πjdt(xjdt)=λjtPjdt(xjdt,x−jdt)Q−∣∣xjdt−Njt∣∣2(16)\Pi_{jdt}(\mathbf{x}_{jdt})=\lambda_{jt}P_{jdt}(\mathbf{x}_{jdt},\mathbf{x}_{-jdt})Q-\left|\left|\mathbf{x}_{jdt}-\mathbf{N}_{jt}\right|\right|^2 \tag{16}Πjdt​(xjdt​)=λjt​Pjdt​(xjdt​,x−jdt​)Q−∣∣xjdt​−Njt​∣∣2(16)

where λjt\lambda_{jt}λjt​ is the weight on electoral incentives relative to alignment with the national platform, so 1/λjt1/\lambda_{jt}1/λjt​ is the relative cost of deviating from the party line and a lower λjt\lambda_{jt}λjt​ means stronger party discipline. Uncertainty comes from an aggregate shock ζjdt∼U(−1ϕ,1ϕ)\zeta_{jdt}\sim U\left(-\frac{1}{\phi},\frac{1}{\phi}\right)ζjdt​∼U(−ϕ1​,ϕ1​) as in probabilistic voting models (Persson and Tabellini 2002), which makes the probability of winning linear in the vote share conditional on turnout:

The derivative of the objective with respect to xjdktx_{jdkt}xjdkt​ is λjtQϕ2\lambda_{jt}Q\frac{\phi}{2}λjt​Q2ϕ​ times the slope of the conditional vote share minus 2(xjdkt−Njkt)2(x_{jdkt}-N_{jkt})2(xjdkt​−Njkt​). Setting it to zero on each dimension and adding a residual gives the equilibrium condition:

(xjdkt−Njkt)=λ~jt∂s~jdt(xjdt,x−jdt)∂xjdkt+ηjdkt(18)\left(x_{jdkt}-N_{jkt}\right)=\tilde{\lambda}_{jt}\frac{\partial\tilde{s}_{jdt}(\mathbf{x}_{jdt},\mathbf{x}_{-jdt})}{\partial x_{jdkt}}+\eta_{jdkt} \tag{18}(xjdkt​−Njkt​)=λ~jt​∂xjdkt​∂s~jdt​(xjdt​,x−jdt​)​+ηjdkt​(18)

with:

λ~jt=λjtϕQ4(19)\tilde{\lambda}_{jt}=\frac{\lambda_{jt}\phi Q}{4} \tag{19}λ~jt​=4λjt​ϕQ​(19)

A candidate deviates from the leadership in the direction in which local voters reward a move, in proportion to the local slope of demand. The term ηjdkt\eta_{jdkt}ηjdkt​ collects candidate-level unobservables and measurement error in positions; it plays the role of the marginal-cost residual in a pricing equation. Only the composite λ~jt\tilde{\lambda}_{jt}λ~jt​ is identified: discipline is measured relative to the rent QQQ and to the support of the shock.

Estimation is conditional on demand. The slope of s~jdt\tilde{s}_{jdt}s~jdt​ is computed from the demand estimates, and the equilibrium condition is a linear regression of deviations from the leadership on that slope, with a nonzero mean allowed for ηjdkt\eta_{jdkt}ηjdkt​. Because the slope is evaluated at the observed position, which depends mechanically on ηjdkt\eta_{jdkt}ηjdkt​, it is instrumented with the slope evaluated at the median candidate position of each party, which keeps the variation that comes from the composition of district voters. Standard errors are reported in a conventional version and in a version adjusted for demand-side estimation uncertainty.

  • 2000-2010: λ~\tilde{\lambda}λ~ is 22.26 for Republicans (conventional standard error 4.11, adjusted 9.34) and 22.66 for Democrats (5.59, adjusted 17.81). In a district where moving one standard deviation to the left raises the vote share by one percentage point, a candidate deviates from the party line by about one quarter of a standard deviation in that direction.

  • 2012-2020: λ~\tilde{\lambda}λ~ is −3.97-3.97−3.97 (3.74, adjusted 6.93) for Republicans and −5.82-5.82−5.82 (3.01, adjusted 6.42) for Democrats, not distinguishable from zero: candidates no longer adapt to local demand, and positions become uniform within each party.

  • Robustness: adding party-by-dimension-by-year fixed effects gives 22.89 and 22.69 in the first period and −0.63-0.63−0.63 and −3.73-3.73−3.73 in the second; excluding party leaders gives 22.92, 21.94, −0.53-0.53−0.53 and −3.40-3.40−3.40.

Party discipline is interpreted broadly: it may reflect pressure from leaders, career concerns, changes in primary electorates or the selection of more aligned candidates. As a robustness check the shock is given a logistic distribution with scale κ\kappaκ, so that the probability of winning is nonlinear in the vote share and uncertainty is concentrated in close races:

Pj(xjt,x−jt)=11+exp⁡(−sj−0.5κ)(20)P_j(\mathbf{x}_{jt},\mathbf{x}_{-jt})=\frac{1}{1+\exp\left(-\frac{s_j-0.5}{\kappa}\right)} \tag{20}Pj​(xjt​,x−jt​)=1+exp(−κsj​−0.5​)1​(20)

For κ\kappaκ equal to 0.1, 0.075 and 0.05 the ratios of the estimates across periods and parties are almost unchanged, and the second-period coefficients become small, positive and more precisely estimated.

Equilibrium and Decomposition

A counterfactual scenario is a set of primitives that delivers an equilibrium:

(x∗,s∗)=f(Fpt(w),βt,Nt,λt∣mt,αt,ξt,ηt)(21)\left(\mathbf{x}^*,\mathbf{s}^*\right)=f\left(F_{pt}(\mathbf{w}),\boldsymbol{\beta}_t,\mathbf{N}_t,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t\mid\mathbf{m}_t,\boldsymbol{\alpha}_t,\boldsymbol{\xi}_t,\boldsymbol{\eta}_t\right) \tag{21}(x∗,s∗)=f(Fpt​(w),βt​,Nt​,λt​∣mt​,αt​,ξt​,ηt​)(21)

where x∗\mathbf{x}^*x∗ and s∗\mathbf{s}^*s∗ are the vectors of candidate positions and vote probabilities, βt\boldsymbol{\beta}_tβt​ are ideological preferences, λt\boldsymbol{\lambda}_tλt​ are the weights on electoral incentives, mt=(mp,d)∀p,d\mathbf{m}_t=(m_{p,d})_{\forall p,d}mt​=(mp,d​)∀p,d​ is the map from precincts to districts, αt\boldsymbol{\alpha}_tαt​ are partisan preferences, ξt\boldsymbol{\xi}_tξt​ are precinct taste shocks and ηt\boldsymbol{\eta}_tηt​ are positioning residuals. In each scenario the equilibrium positions solve a fixed point in which each candidate plays the best response implied by the equilibrium condition to the position of the opponent; the fixed point is computed with the imitation game algorithm of McLennan and Tourky (2005). The resulting positions are fed into the demand system to obtain vote probabilities. The paper refers to the equilibrium of a scenario as unique and gives no formal proof.

Five factors are evaluated at their initial (2000-2010) or final (2012-2020) values: the demographic distribution Ft(w)F_t(\mathbf{w})Ft​(w), voter preferences βt\boldsymbol{\beta}_tβt​, the cultural leadership positions Ncult\mathbf{N}_{cult}Ncult​, the economic leadership positions Necon\mathbf{N}_{econ}Necon​, and party discipline λt\boldsymbol{\lambda}_tλt​. Two nuisance factors that also change, overall partisanship α\boldsymbol{\alpha}α and the district map m\mathbf{m}m, are included, which gives 27=1282^7=12827=128 scenarios. Because the effect of each factor depends on the values of the others, contributions are averaged with a Shapley value decomposition. For each factor zzz, the contribution to the change in the probability sij(⋅)s_{ij}(\cdot)sij​(⋅) that voter iii votes for the Democratic candidate is:

ϕi(z)=1n∑C(n−1∣C∣)−1(sij(⋅,zfinal)−sij(⋅,zinitial))(22)\phi_i(z)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_C\binom{n-1}{|C|}^{-1}\left(s_{ij}(\cdot,z_{final})-s_{ij}(\cdot,z_{initial})\right) \tag{22}ϕi​(z)=n1​C∑​(∣C∣n−1​)−1(sij​(⋅,zfinal​)−sij​(⋅,zinitial​))(22)

where the sum runs over the coalitions CCC that do not include zzz, a coalition being the set of factors evaluated at their final values, and n=7n=7n=7. Contributions are averaged over individuals separately for more-educated and less-educated voters. Each contribution includes the direct effect of the factor and the indirect effect through endogenous candidate positions.

Decomposition Results

The outcome is the education gap in Democratic voting, the probability that a voter with above-median education votes for the Democratic candidate minus that of a voter with below-median education. The gap increased by 7.4 percentage points between the two periods. The contributions below are read from the figures of the paper and are approximate.

  • Cultural positions of the leadership: the largest positive contribution, about +0.9+0.9+0.9 percentage points. Cultural polarization lowers the Democratic vote probability of less-educated voters by about 0.6 points and raises that of more-educated voters by about 0.4 points.

  • Economic positions of the leadership: a small negative contribution, about −0.1-0.1−0.1 points, which only partly offsets the cultural effect.

  • Voter preferences: the largest negative contribution, about −1.2-1.2−1.2 points. The change in βt\boldsymbol{\beta}_tβt​ raises the Democratic vote probability of less-educated voters by about 1.7 points and that of more-educated voters by about 0.6 points, because less-educated voters became more progressive on economic issues.

  • Demographics: a small negative contribution, about −0.05-0.05−0.05 points.

  • Party discipline: approximately zero. Discipline rose in both parties and limited local adaptation by both candidates, changing Democratic vote probabilities by similar amounts in the two groups.

  • Unexplained part: the five factors together account for a small share of the 7.4 points. Most of the change is captured by αijt\alpha_{ijt}αijt​, which contains non-ideological partisanship and the positions of presidential, Senate and party leaders. If these operate through the same ideological channels, the estimated supply-side effect is a lower bound.

The mechanism is the changing balance of polarization and not polarization as such. In the early 2000s the parties were about equally polarized on the two dimensions. Since then they diverged on cultural issues only, so less-educated voters, who are culturally conservative and economically progressive, derive less utility from Democratic candidates, and more-educated voters derive more. Had economic polarization increased along with cultural polarization, realignment by education would have been less pronounced. The decline of class voting is thus not due to less-educated voters abandoning progressive economic policy; their support for it increased.

This is the definition of the individual choice probability in a discrete-choice model of voting. Voter iii in district ddd at election ttt has three alternatives: the Democratic candidate DDD, the Republican candidate RRR, and abstention 000. The utility of a candidate is uijdt=vit(xjdt;widt)+εijdtu_{ijdt}=v_{it}(\mathbf{x}_{jdt};\mathbf{w}_{idt})+\varepsilon_{ijdt}uijdt​=vit​(xjdt​;widt​)+εijdt​ and that of abstention is ui0dt=εi0dtu_{i0dt}=\varepsilon_{i0dt}ui0dt​=εi0dt​, so the systematic utility of abstention is normalized to zero. The probability is taken over the idiosyncratic shocks εijdt\varepsilon_{ijdt}εijdt​, which the econometrician and the candidates do not observe; given the shocks the voter's choice is deterministic.

Writing the event out for j=Dj=Dj=D shows what matters:

siDdt=Pr⁡(εiRdt−εiDdt≤vit(xDdt)−vit(xRdt),  εi0dt−εiDdt≤vit(xDdt))s_{iDdt}=\Pr\left(\varepsilon_{iRdt}-\varepsilon_{iDdt}\leq v_{it}(\mathbf{x}_{Ddt})-v_{it}(\mathbf{x}_{Rdt}),\ \ \varepsilon_{i0dt}-\varepsilon_{iDdt}\leq v_{it}(\mathbf{x}_{Ddt})\right)siDdt​=Pr(εiRdt​−εiDdt​≤vit​(xDdt​)−vit​(xRdt​),  εi0dt​−εiDdt​≤vit​(xDdt​))

Only utility differences enter, and the three probabilities sum to one. The probability depends on both platforms xDdt\mathbf{x}_{Ddt}xDdt​ and xRdt\mathbf{x}_{Rdt}xRdt​, which is what creates strategic interaction between the candidates, and on the observable characteristics widt\mathbf{w}_{idt}widt​, which is what lets groups react differently to the same platforms. Because abstention is an alternative, a platform can win votes both by persuasion (taking voters from the opponent) and by mobilization (taking voters from abstention). No distribution is imposed at this stage; with type-I extreme value shocks the probability takes the logit form used in equation (11). The probability is aggregated to the district in equation (2) and enters the candidate's objective in equation (3).

The district vote share of alternative jjj is the average of the individual choice probabilities of equation (1) over the voters of the district. Since the idiosyncratic shocks are independent across a large number of voters, the realized share equals the expected share, and the expectation is taken over the distribution Fdt(⋅)F_{dt}(\cdot)Fdt​(⋅) of observable characteristics w\mathbf{w}w in district ddd at election ttt. With a finite number of voter types w1,…,wG\mathbf{w}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{w}_Gw1​,…,wG​ with population weights πgdt\pi_{gdt}πgdt​ the integral is a weighted sum:

sjdt=∑g=1Gπgdt sijdt(xDdt,xRdt;wg),sDdt+sRdt+s0dt=1s_{jdt}=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\pi_{gdt}\,s_{ijdt}\left(\mathbf{x}_{Ddt},\mathbf{x}_{Rdt};\mathbf{w}_g\right),\qquad s_{Ddt}+s_{Rdt}+s_{0dt}=1sjdt​=g=1∑G​πgdt​sijdt​(xDdt​,xRdt​;wg​),sDdt​+sRdt​+s0dt​=1

The equation separates the two demand-side objects of the decomposition. A share can change because the function sijdt(⋅)s_{ijdt}(\cdot)sijdt​(⋅) changes, that is, the same type of voter responds differently to the same platforms (preferences), or because FdtF_{dt}Fdt​ changes, that is, the mix of types changes (demographics). Shares defined this way are fractions of the voting-age population, so s0dts_{0dt}s0dt​ is the abstention rate. The object that decides the election is the share conditional on turnout:

s~jdt=sjdtsDdt+sRdt\tilde{s}_{jdt}=\frac{s_{jdt}}{s_{Ddt}+s_{Rdt}}s~jdt​=sDdt​+sRdt​sjdt​​

which is the argument of the winning probability in equation (17). The empirical counterpart of the integral, with a parametric choice probability and with precincts in place of districts, is equation (11).

This is the generic objective of candidate jjj in the conceptual framework. The first term is the expected benefit of running: the probability of winning PjdtP_{jdt}Pjdt​ times the rent from office Q>0Q>0Q>0. The second term cjt(xjdt,Njt)c_{jt}(\mathbf{x}_{jdt},\mathbf{N}_{jt})cjt​(xjdt​,Njt​) is the cost of choosing a platform different from the position Njt\mathbf{N}_{jt}Njt​ of the national party leadership; it is indexed by party and period, so discipline can differ between parties and change over time, but it is the same for all districts. The opponent's platform x−jdt\mathbf{x}_{-jdt}x−jdt​ enters only through the winning probability, so the game between the two candidates of a district is a game of electoral competition with a private cost of positioning.

The candidate is purely office-motivated: the platform has no intrinsic value to the candidate, and all policy motivation is folded into the cost of leaving the party line. Without the cost, both candidates would move to the vote-maximizing platform and the positions of the leadership would be irrelevant; with an infinite cost, every candidate would sit at Njt\mathbf{N}_{jt}Njt​ and local voters would be irrelevant. The interior trade-off is what the supply side estimates.

The parametric version is equation (16), which is written as λjtPjdtQ−∣∣xjdt−Njt∣∣2\lambda_{jt}P_{jdt}Q-||\mathbf{x}_{jdt}-\mathbf{N}_{jt}||^2λjt​Pjdt​Q−∣∣xjdt​−Njt​∣∣2. This is a descriptive regression that ranks demographic variables by how much their relationship with the Democratic vote has shifted. The unit is a precinct ppp at election ttt; the outcome S~Dpt\tilde{S}_{Dpt}S~Dpt​ is the observed Democratic share of the two-party House vote, that is, conditional on turnout. Each of the M=12M=12M=12 variables wm,ptw_{m,pt}wm,pt​ is standardized, so coefficients are comparable across variables. The coefficient γm\gamma_mγm​ is the level gradient of variable mmm at t=0t=0t=0, and βm\beta_mβm​ is the change of that gradient per unit of ttt:

∂S~Dpt∂wm,pt=γm+βmt\frac{\partial\tilde{S}_{Dpt}}{\partial w_{m,pt}}=\gamma_m+\beta_m t∂wm,pt​∂S~Dpt​​=γm​+βm​t

A positive βm\beta_mβm​ means that precincts with a high value of wmw_mwm​ are moving toward the Democrats relative to precincts with a low value, which is the definition of realignment along dimension mmm. The election fixed effects μt\mu_tμt​ absorb national swings, so only the cross-section of precincts within each election is used. Putting all twelve variables in one regression makes each βm\beta_mβm​ a partial trend: the education coefficient is the shift by education holding the trends by income, race, rurality and the others fixed.

The regression is not causal and is not part of the structural model; it documents the fact that the model later decomposes, namely that education has the largest ∣βm∣|\beta_m|∣βm​∣. Since it uses precinct averages, it is an ecological regression: it shows how the gradient across precincts moves, not how individual voters move, which is one reason the structural demand model of equations (9) to (11) integrates over the within-precinct distribution of demographics.

This is the two-parameter logistic item-response model for a binary survey item qqq (for example, support or opposition to a policy). The latent position xjktx_{jkt}xjkt​ of candidate jjj on dimension kkk is the only candidate-specific determinant of the answer; the item contributes a cut-point βq\beta_qβq​ and a discrimination parameter αq>0\alpha_q>0αq​>0. The log odds of a yes are linear in the position:

log⁡Pr⁡(yjqt=1)Pr⁡(yjqt=0)=αq(xjkt−βq)\log\frac{\Pr\left(y_{jqt}=1\right)}{\Pr\left(y_{jqt}=0\right)}=\alpha_q\left(x_{jkt}-\beta_q\right)logPr(yjqt​=0)Pr(yjqt​=1)​=αq​(xjkt​−βq​)

At xjkt=βqx_{jkt}=\beta_qxjkt​=βq​ the probability is one half, so βq\beta_qβq​ locates the item on the ideological scale: an item with a high βq\beta_qβq​ is one to which only very conservative candidates say yes. The slope of the probability with respect to the position is

∂Pr⁡(yjqt=1)∂xjkt=αqPr⁡(yjqt=1)[1−Pr⁡(yjqt=1)]\frac{\partial\Pr\left(y_{jqt}=1\right)}{\partial x_{jkt}}=\alpha_q\Pr\left(y_{jqt}=1\right)\left[1-\Pr\left(y_{jqt}=1\right)\right]∂xjkt​∂Pr(yjqt​=1)​=αq​Pr(yjqt​=1)[1−Pr(yjqt​=1)]

which is at most αq/4\alpha_q/4αq​/4, reached at the cut-point. A large αq\alpha_qαq​ means the item separates candidates sharply around βq\beta_qβq​ and is very informative about positions near it; αq\alpha_qαq​ close to zero means the answer is nearly unrelated to the dimension. With αq>0\alpha_q>0αq​>0 the item is coded so that a yes is the high-position answer. Each item is assigned to one dimension (economic or cultural) by its topic, so the two dimensions are defined by the classification of items and not by a rotation. Location and scale of the latent positions are not identified by this equation alone, since αq(xjkt−βq)\alpha_q(x_{jkt}-\beta_q)αq​(xjkt​−βq​) is unchanged if positions and cut-points are shifted together or rescaled with αq\alpha_qαq​; the unit-variance prior of equation (7) fixes them. The ordered counterpart is equation (6).

This is the graded response model for an ordered item with CqC_qCq​ categories, coded here as 0,1,…,Cq−10,1,\ldots,C_q-10,1,…,Cq​−1. It applies the binary model of equation (5) to each of the Cq−1C_q-1Cq​−1 cumulative splits "answer at least ccc" versus "answer below ccc", with a common discrimination parameter αq\alpha_qαq​ and a separate cut-point δqc\delta_{qc}δqc​ for each split. The probability of each single category is the difference of adjacent cumulative probabilities, with the conventions Pr⁡(yjqt≥0)=1\Pr(y_{jqt}\geq0)=1Pr(yjqt​≥0)=1 and Pr⁡(yjqt≥Cq)=0\Pr(y_{jqt}\geq C_q)=0Pr(yjqt​≥Cq​)=0:

The ordering δq1<⋯<δq,Cq−1\delta_{q1}<\cdots<\delta_{q,C_q-1}δq1​<⋯<δq,Cq​−1​ is what guarantees that these differences are positive: a higher threshold is harder to pass, so its cumulative probability is lower at every position. The common αq\alpha_qαq​ makes the cumulative curves parallel in log odds, the proportional-odds assumption. Each δqc\delta_{qc}δqc​ is the position at which a candidate is equally likely to answer below ccc or at least ccc. With Cq=2C_q=2Cq​=2 there is one cut-point and the model is exactly equation (5) with βq=δq1\beta_q=\delta_{q1}βq​=δq1​.

Using the ordered information instead of collapsing answers into two groups keeps the intensity of the response: a candidate who strongly agrees is placed further out than one who somewhat agrees. The likelihood of the survey data is the product over candidates, items and periods of the probabilities in equations (5) and (6), combined with the prior on the path of positions in equation (7).

The first line is an assumed first-order autoregressive law of motion for the latent position; the second line contains two results, the mapping from the half-life to the persistence and the innovation scale that delivers a unit stationary variance.

Half-life. Iterating the first line hhh periods forward and taking expectations, a deviation of the position decays geometrically:

E[xjk,t+h∣xjkt]=ρkhxjkt\mathbb{E}\left[x_{jk,t+h}\mid x_{jkt}\right]=\rho_k^{h}x_{jkt}E[xjk,t+h​∣xjkt​]=ρkh​xjkt​

The half-life hkh_khk​ is the horizon at which half of the deviation remains, so it solves

ρkhk=12⟹hklog⁡ρk=−log⁡2⟹ρk=2−1/hk\rho_k^{h_k}=\frac{1}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h_k\log\rho_k=-\log2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\rho_k=2^{-1/h_k}ρkhk​​=21​⟹hk​logρk​=−log2⟹ρk​=2−1/hk​

Any hk>0h_k>0hk​>0 gives 0<ρk<10<\rho_k<10<ρk​<1. With hk=1h_k=1hk​=1 election cycle, the centre of the prior, ρk=0.5\rho_k=0.5ρk​=0.5.

Unit variance. Since ηjkt\eta_{jkt}ηjkt​ is independent of xjk,t−1x_{jk,t-1}xjk,t−1​ and has unit variance, taking variances of the first line gives

Var⁡(xjkt)=ρk2Var⁡(xjk,t−1)+σk2\operatorname{Var}\left(x_{jkt}\right)=\rho_k^2\operatorname{Var}\left(x_{jk,t-1}\right)+\sigma_k^2Var(xjkt​)=ρk2​Var(xjk,t−1​)+σk2​

In a stationary distribution the variance is the same in both periods, call it VVV, so

V=ρk2V+σk2⟹V=σk21−ρk2V=\rho_k^2V+\sigma_k^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad V=\frac{\sigma_k^2}{1-\rho_k^2}V=ρk2​V+σk2​⟹V=1−ρk2​σk2​​

Requiring V=1V=1V=1 gives

The mean is zero because the process has no intercept. Hence, if the initial position is drawn from N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1)N(0,1), every xjktx_{jkt}xjkt​ is marginally N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1)N(0,1): positions are measured in cross-sectional standard deviations, which fixes the location and scale left open by equations (5) and (6). With hk=1h_k=1hk​=1, σk=0.75≈0.87\sigma_k=\sqrt{0.75}\approx0.87σk​=0.75​≈0.87. The correlation of a candidate's positions hhh cycles apart is ρkh\rho_k^{h}ρkh​, so the prior shrinks a candidate's position in a cycle with few answers toward that candidate's positions in neighbouring cycles, and by less the further apart they are.

The weight in the second line is the one that minimizes the variance of the combined measure when the two measures are treated as unbiased, independent noisy signals of the same true position xjdkt∗x^{*}_{jdkt}xjdkt∗​. Write

which is smaller than either variance. A candidate who answered few items has a large standard error and is placed mostly by the website; when only one measure exists it is used alone. The independence of the two errors is an assumption that the paper and the note do not state. Because the website model is trained to predict survey ideal points, its error can be correlated with the survey error, in which case the formula is an approximation to the optimal weight.

This is the indirect utility of voter iii, living in precinct ppp of district ddd, from voting for candidate j∈{D,R}j\in\{D,R\}j∈{D,R} at election ttt. It has four parts. The term ∑kβiktxjdkt\sum_k\beta_{ikt}x_{jdkt}∑k​βikt​xjdkt​ is the ideological utility: xjdktx_{jdkt}xjdkt​ is the position of the candidate on dimension kkk (cultural or economic), which is common to all precincts of the district, and βikt\beta_{ikt}βikt​ is the voter's marginal utility of a higher position. The term αijt\alpha_{ijt}αijt​ is the utility of voting for party jjj that does not depend on the House candidate's positions. The term ξjpt\xi_{jpt}ξjpt​ is a party-specific shock common to all voters of the precinct and unobserved by the econometrician, the analogue of unobserved product quality in demand estimation. The term εijpt\varepsilon_{ijpt}εijpt​ is the type-I extreme value idiosyncratic shock. Abstention has systematic utility zero, so all parameters are measured relative to not voting.

The model is a demand system in which candidates are products and positions are characteristics. Utility is linear in positions, not a distance to an ideal point: a voter with βikt>0\beta_{ikt}>0βikt​>0 always prefers a higher position on kkk. Since higher values are more conservative (the sign convention is inferred from the estimates: the interaction of the cultural position with schooling is negative and the paper reads it as educated voters preferring progressive cultural positions), βikt>0\beta_{ikt}>0βikt​>0 is a taste for conservative positions. What decides the choice between the two candidates is

uiDpt−uiRpt=∑kβikt(xDdkt−xRdkt)+αiDt−αiRt+ξDpt−ξRpt+εiDpt−εiRptu_{iDpt}-u_{iRpt}=\sum_k\beta_{ikt}\left(x_{Ddkt}-x_{Rdkt}\right)+\alpha_{iDt}-\alpha_{iRt}+\xi_{Dpt}-\xi_{Rpt}+\varepsilon_{iDpt}-\varepsilon_{iRpt}uiDpt​−uiRpt​=k∑​βikt​(xDdkt​−xRdkt​)+αiDt​−αiRt​+ξDpt​−ξRpt​+εiDpt​−εiRpt​

so only the distance between the candidates on each dimension matters for the two-party split, which is why the education-neutral curve is drawn in the plane of polarization on the two dimensions. The levels of the positions matter for turnout. Linearity can be seen as a local approximation of spatial preferences, and it implies that a voter never prefers an interior platform. The coefficients are specified in equation (10) and the shares in equation (11).

These two lines specify how preferences vary across voters. In the first, the party preference αijt\alpha_{ijt}αijt​ has a baseline αjt\alpha_{jt}αjt​ and a gradient αjtw\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{w}}_{jt}αjtw​ in the demographics wit\mathbf{w}_{it}wit​ (years of schooling, a white indicator, age). In the second, the ideological coefficient βikt\beta_{ikt}βikt​ on dimension kkk has a baseline βkt\beta_{kt}βkt​, a demographic gradient βktw\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}βktw​ and an unobserved component σktβνkit\sigma^{\beta}_{kt}\nu_{kit}σktβ​νkit​ with νkit\nu_{kit}νkit​ standard normal and independent across dimensions. All parameters carry a ttt subscript because separate models are estimated for 2000-2010 and 2012-2020; the change in βkt\beta_{kt}βkt​, βktw\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}βktw​ and σktβ\sigma^{\beta}_{kt}σktβ​ between the periods is the preference factor of the decomposition, while the change in the party terms is treated as a nuisance factor.

The gradients are the parameters of interest. Realignment by education through ideology requires that the marginal utility of positions depends on schooling; the element of βktw\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}βktw​ on schooling is βedu,cult\beta_{edu,cult}βedu,cult​ or βedu,econ\beta_{edu,econ}βedu,econ​. As an illustration with the first-period estimates of the paper's Table 1 (which also reports an age interaction of 0.00090.00090.0009), a white voter of mean age 48.9148.9148.91 with eee years of schooling and νkit=0\nu_{kit}=0νkit​=0 has a cultural coefficient of

which is positive below about 13.613.613.6 years of schooling and negative above: such voters reward culturally conservative candidates if they have less than some college and penalize them otherwise. The baseline βkt\beta_{kt}βkt​ alone is the coefficient of a hypothetical voter with all demographics equal to zero and has no direct interpretation.

The random coefficient σktβνkit\sigma^{\beta}_{kt}\nu_{kit}σktβ​νkit​ lets voters with identical demographics disagree and relaxes the substitution patterns of the plain logit. This is the inversion of Berry (1994) in closed form: the unobserved shock is the residual of a linear equation, with two observations (one per party) for each precinct-election and the log of the party's share of the voting-age population relative to the abstention share as the dependent variable. The demographic gradients are the coefficients on the interactions of positions with precinct averages. The cost is the one stressed by the Monte Carlo evidence: when voters within a precinct differ, the log of an average of logit probabilities is not the logit of the average voter, so the gradients estimated from precinct means are biased, and more so for larger units such as counties.

This equation splits the precinct taste shock into three parts in order to state which variation in candidate positions is used. The problem is that positions xjdktx_{jdkt}xjdkt​ are chosen by candidates who know the tastes of their district, so they are correlated with ξjpt\xi_{jpt}ξjpt​, exactly as prices are correlated with unobserved quality in demand estimation. The first component ξjg(p)t\xi_{jg(p)t}ξjg(p)t​ is common, for party jjj and election ttt, to the small group g(p)g(p)g(p) of adjacent precincts that straddles a congressional district border. The second component ξjp\xi_{jp}ξjp​ is the permanent attachment of precinct ppp to party jjj. The third, ξ~jpt\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}ξ~​jpt​, is what remains.

The first two components are removed with fixed effects (group by party by election, and precinct by party). The variation left in positions is of the difference-in-differences type. Take two precincts ppp and p′p'p′ of the same group on opposite sides of a border, in districts ddd and d′d'd′, and two elections ttt and t′t't′; after the fixed effects the positions enter only through

(xjdkt−xjd′kt)−(xjdkt′−xjd′kt′)\left(x_{jdkt}-x_{jd'kt}\right)-\left(x_{jdkt'}-x_{jd'kt'}\right)(xjdkt​−xjd′kt​)−(xjdkt′​−xjd′kt′​)

that is, the change over time in the difference between the candidates that two neighbouring precincts face. A precinct is about one four-hundredth of a district, so a candidate does not tailor the platform to one border precinct, and whatever the candidate responds to at the level of the local area is shared by the neighbours across the border and absorbed by ξjg(p)t\xi_{jg(p)t}ξjg(p)t​. The identifying assumption, used in equation (14), is that the residual ξ~jpt\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}ξ~​jpt​ is uncorrelated with positions. It would fail if the two sides of a border experienced different taste shocks that the candidates respond to, which the balance test on demographics is meant to address. The group fixed effects also absorb the variation in demographics within a group, which is why the party gradients are estimated in a second step with equation (15).

These are the first-step GMM moment conditions. Each says that an instrument is uncorrelated with the residual taste shock ξ~jpt\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}ξ~​jpt​ of equation (13), that is, with the shock recovered from the inversion of equation (11) after partialling out the group-by-party-by-election and precinct-by-party fixed effects. They are not derived from the model; they are the exogeneity assumption of the border design, written for one instrument at a time, for each dimension kkk, each characteristic wptw_{pt}wpt​ and each party jjj.

The first three rows are the moments for the linear part: the position itself identifies the baseline βkt\beta_{kt}βkt​, its interaction with demographics identifies the gradients βktw\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}βktw​, and the demographics are controls. Positions are their own instruments because, after the fixed effects, they are assumed exogenous. The last four rows add functions of the positions that are excluded from the mean utility: the square of the own position, the distance between the two candidates xDdkt−xRdktx_{Ddkt}-x_{Rdkt}xDdkt​−xRdkt​, and their interactions with demographics. They are valid under the same assumption and they are what identifies the nonlinear parameters σktβ\sigma^{\beta}_{kt}σktβ​ and separates gradients across individuals from gradients across precincts: with heterogeneous voters, the response of shares to a position is not log-linear and depends on the opponent's position, and the curvature and the cross-candidate response are informative about the dispersion of βikt\beta_{ikt}βikt​. In a homogeneous logit these extra instruments would be redundant, since equation (12) is linear.

The sample analogue for an instrument zjptz_{jpt}zjpt​ is

and the estimator minimizes a quadratic form in the stacked moments. No micro moments are used, so the identification of individual heterogeneity relies on the within-precinct demographic distributions and on functional form.

This is the moment condition of the second estimation step. The first step, with the fixed effects of equation (13), cannot recover how the party preference αijt\alpha_{ijt}αijt​ varies with demographics, because the precincts of a border group have nearly identical demographics, wpt≈wg(p)tw_{pt}\approx w_{g(p)t}wpt​≈wg(p)t​, and a term such as wpt′αjtw\mathbf{w}'_{pt}\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{w}}_{jt}wpt′​αjtw​ is absorbed by the group-by-party-by-election effect. The second step therefore uses all precincts, not only those at borders, holds the ideological parameters βkt\beta_{kt}βkt​, βktw\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}βktw​ and σktβ\sigma^{\beta}_{kt}σktβ​ at their first-step values, inverts the shares again, and chooses αjt\alpha_{jt}αjt​ and αjtw\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{w}}_{jt}αjtw​ so that the full shock ξjpt\xi_{jpt}ξjpt​ (not the residual ξ~jpt\tilde{\xi}_{jpt}ξ~​jpt​) is uncorrelated with demographics.

In a homogeneous logit the step would be an OLS regression of the mean utility net of the ideological part on demographics:

δjpt−∑k(βkt+wpt′βktw)xjdkt=αjt+wpt′αjtw+ξjpt\delta_{jpt}-\sum_k\left(\beta_{kt}+\mathbf{w}'_{pt}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}\right)x_{jdkt}=\alpha_{jt}+\mathbf{w}'_{pt}\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{w}}_{jt}+\xi_{jpt}δjpt​−k∑​(βkt​+wpt′​βktw​)xjdkt​=αjt​+wpt′​αjtw​+ξjpt​

The assumption is that demographics are exogenous to party taste shocks, a much weaker design than the border comparison. For this reason the party gradients are descriptive: they say how much more a group votes for a party than its ideological preferences and the House candidates' positions predict, including attachment to the party and the coattails of presidential and Senate candidates. They are treated as controls and enter the decomposition as a nuisance factor. Because the second step conditions on estimated first-step parameters, its standard errors are corrected following Murphy and Topel (1985).

The quadratic form buys three things. The marginal cost of deviating, 2(xjdkt−Njkt)2(x_{jdkt}-N_{jkt})2(xjdkt​−Njkt​), is linear, so the first-order condition in equation (18) is linear in the deviation and can be estimated by a regression. The cost is additively separable and symmetric across dimensions, so a deviation on cultural issues costs the same as one on economic issues and does not change the marginal cost on the other dimension. And the cost is strictly convex, which helps the objective to be concave. What it rules out is a dimension-specific discipline and asymmetric costs of deviating to the left or to the right. The parameter is indexed by party and period but not by district or candidate, so incumbents, challengers and candidates in safe or contested seats are assumed to face the same trade-off; candidate-level differences go into the residual of equation (18). The winning probability is specified in equation (17).

This schematic equation states what a counterfactual scenario is. The mapping fff takes the primitives of the model and returns the equilibrium platforms x∗\mathbf{x}^*x∗ of all candidates and the vote probabilities s∗\mathbf{s}^*s∗ of all voters. The arguments before the bar are the factors of economic interest: the demographic distribution Fpt(w)F_{pt}(\mathbf{w})Fpt​(w) and the ideological preferences βt\boldsymbol{\beta}_tβt​ (the parameters βkt\beta_{kt}βkt​, βktw\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{w}}_{kt}βktw​ and σktβ\sigma^{\beta}_{kt}σktβ​ of equation (10)) on the demand side, and the leadership positions Nt\mathbf{N}_tNt​ and the electoral weights λt\boldsymbol{\lambda}_tλt​ (in practice the composites of equation (19)) on the supply side. The arguments after the bar are also needed to solve the model: the map mt\mathbf{m}_tmt​ from precincts to districts, the partisan preferences αt\boldsymbol{\alpha}_tαt​, the taste shocks ξt\boldsymbol{\xi}_tξt​ and the positioning residuals ηt\boldsymbol{\eta}_tηt​.

The mapping is computed in two layers. Given platforms, demand is equation (11) aggregated to districts with mt\mathbf{m}_tmt​. Given demand, platforms solve the system of first-order conditions of equation (18) for both candidates and both dimensions in every district:

xjdk∗=Njk+λ~j∂s~jd(xjd∗,x−jd∗)∂xjdk+ηjdk,j∈{D,R},  k∈{cult,econ}x^*_{jdk}=N_{jk}+\tilde{\lambda}_{j}\frac{\partial\tilde{s}_{jd}\left(\mathbf{x}^*_{jd},\mathbf{x}^*_{-jd}\right)}{\partial x_{jdk}}+\eta_{jdk},\qquad j\in\{D,R\},\ \ k\in\{cult,econ\}xjdk∗​=Njk​+λ~j​∂xjdk​∂s~jd​(xjd∗​,x−jd∗​)​+ηjdk​,j∈{D,R},  k∈{cult,econ}

which is a fixed point because the slope depends on both platforms. Districts are linked only through the common primitives, so the system is solved district by district.

Two features matter for interpretation. A factor has a direct effect and an indirect effect: changing βt\boldsymbol{\beta}_tβt​ changes votes at given platforms and also changes the slope of demand and hence the platforms; changing Nt\mathbf{N}_tNt​ or λt\boldsymbol{\lambda}_tλt​ affects votes only through the platforms, since utility does not depend on the leadership directly. And the residuals ξt\boldsymbol{\xi}_tξt​ and ηt\boldsymbol{\eta}_tηt​ are kept, so the scenario with all factors at the values of a period reproduces the observed positions and shares of that period. Uniqueness of the fixed point is assumed, not proved. Evaluating fff at all combinations of initial and final values gives the scenarios averaged in equation (22).

Δz(C)=v(C∪{z})−v(C)=sij(⋅,zfinal)−sij(⋅,zinitial)\Delta_z(C)=v\left(C\cup\{z\}\right)-v(C)=s_{ij}(\cdot,z_{final})-s_{ij}(\cdot,z_{initial})Δz​(C)=v(C∪{z})−v(C)=sij​(⋅,zfinal​)−sij​(⋅,zinitial​)

where the dot stands for the configuration CCC of the other six factors.

Step 1: average over orderings. Switch the factors one at a time in some order; the contribution of zzz in that order is Δz(C)\Delta_z(C)Δz​(C) with CCC the set of factors switched before zzz. The Shapley value is the average over all n!n!n! orders, which treats the factors symmetrically:

ϕi(z)=1n!∑ordersΔz(Corder)\phi_i(z)=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\text{orders}}\Delta_z\left(C_{\text{order}}\right)ϕi​(z)=n!1​orders∑​Δz​(Corder​)

Step 2: count orders. A given coalition CCC is the set of predecessors of zzz in ∣C∣! (n−1−∣C∣)!|C|!\,(n-1-|C|)!∣C∣!(n−1−∣C∣)! orders: the members of CCC can be arranged in ∣C∣!|C|!∣C∣! ways before zzz and the remaining n−1−∣C∣n-1-|C|n−1−∣C∣ factors in (n−1−∣C∣)!(n-1-|C|)!(n−1−∣C∣)! ways after it. Grouping the orders by CCC:

ϕi(z)=∑C∌z∣C∣!(n−1−∣C∣)!n!Δz(C)\phi_i(z)=\sum_{C\not\ni z}\frac{|C|!\left(n-1-|C|\right)!}{n!}\Delta_z(C)ϕi​(z)=C∋z∑​n!∣C∣!(n−1−∣C∣)!​Δz​(C)

Step 3: rewrite the weight with a binomial coefficient, using n!=n (n−1)!n!=n\,(n-1)!n!=n(n−1)!:

∣C∣!(n−1−∣C∣)!n!=1n⋅∣C∣!(n−1−∣C∣)!(n−1)!=1n(n−1∣C∣)−1\frac{|C|!\left(n-1-|C|\right)!}{n!}=\frac{1}{n}\cdot\frac{|C|!\left(n-1-|C|\right)!}{(n-1)!}=\frac{1}{n}\binom{n-1}{|C|}^{-1}n!∣C∣!(n−1−∣C∣)!​=n1​⋅(n−1)!∣C∣!(n−1−∣C∣)!​=n1​(∣C∣n−1​)−1

which gives the equation:

ϕi(z)=1n∑C∌z(n−1∣C∣)−1(sij(⋅,zfinal)−sij(⋅,zinitial))\phi_i(z)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{C\not\ni z}\binom{n-1}{|C|}^{-1}\left(s_{ij}(\cdot,z_{final})-s_{ij}(\cdot,z_{initial})\right)ϕi​(z)=n1​C∋z∑​(∣C∣n−1​)−1(sij​(⋅,zfinal​)−sij​(⋅,zinitial​))

The weights sum to one: there are (n−1c)\binom{n-1}{c}(cn−1​) coalitions of size ccc, so each size c=0,…,n−1c=0,\ldots,n-1c=0,…,n−1 receives total weight 1/n1/n1/n. With n=7n=7n=7 a factor has 26=642^6=6426=64 coalitions (each using two of the 128 scenarios), and the weight of a single coalition of size 0,1,2,30,1,2,30,1,2,3 is 17,142,1105,1140\frac{1}{7},\frac{1}{42},\frac{1}{105},\frac{1}{140}71​,421​,1051​,1401​, symmetric for sizes 6,5,46,5,46,5,4.

Adding up. Along any order the contributions telescope to the total change, so the average does too:

∑zϕi(z)=v(all)−v(∅)\sum_{z}\phi_i(z)=v(\text{all})-v(\varnothing)z∑​ϕi​(z)=v(all)−v(∅)

The seven contributions therefore sum exactly to the change in the model probability, with no interaction residual. The five reported contributions do not sum to it, because the two nuisance factors (partisanship and the district map) are part of the seven. The formula is linear in the outcome, so averaging ϕi(z)\phi_i(z)ϕi​(z) over the voters of a group gives the contribution to the group's vote probability, and the difference between the more-educated and less-educated groups gives the contribution to the education gap.
